chunks: "Pipelining is overlapping the execution of several instructions by splitting the datapath into stages and putting registers between the stages.
The classic analogy is a laundry line: while the first load is in the dryer, the second is already in the washer.
Each load still takes the same total time, but a finished load comes out every time the slowest machine finishes, instead of every time the whole job finishes.
In a CPU, I'd cut the instruction path into fetch, decode, execute, memory and writeback.
Without pipelining, the clock period has to cover the entire path, so say 900 picoseconds.
With five stages, each is a fifth of the work, so the clock only needs to cover the slowest stage plus the register overhead, about 270 picoseconds in my example.
Once the pipeline is full, one instruction completes every cycle. What I'd stress is that latency doesn't improve.
One instruction actually takes slightly longer, five cycles of 270 instead of one of 900. What improves is throughput.

And it's never a perfect five times, because the stages aren't balanced, the registers add overhead, and hazards force stalls when one instruction depends on another or a branch changes the fetch address.
That's why you see forwarding paths and branch predictors in every real pipelined design."
